Kishore: You're quiet today, Sudha. Something on your mind?
Sudha: Yes, Papa. Can I ask about Saturday evenings? Not if you're tired.
Kishore: I'm fine. On Sundays I'm human.
Sudha: I know. That's why I waited. On Thursday you had the audit and came home with a headache, and after my maths result on Friday I didn't want to add anything.
Kishore: You planned this?
Sudha: I did. The same question on Thursday could have got a no. Today you've had lunch and tea.
Kishore: (laughs) Fair enough. Go on.
Sudha: I'd like to stay at Devi's until eight on Saturdays. I'll give you the address and call when I arrive.
Kishore: Let me speak to your mother. But thank you for asking like this.

qa.q: Which day did Sudha choose to ask Papa?
qa.a: Sudha chose Sunday, after lunch and tea.

qa.q: What is Sudha worried about that makes Sudha wait?
qa.a: Sudha worries that a request at a tired or upsetting moment would get a no, and wants a fair hearing.

qa.q: What else could Sudha do to help Kishore agree, and why?
qa.a: Sudha could offer to introduce Devi's parents or suggest a short trial, because concrete details answer a father's likely worries.

qa.q: How does Kishore see the way Sudha asked?
qa.a: Kishore is amused and touched that Sudha thought about the timing, and takes the request seriously.

grounding: The teen avoids raising the request when the father is tired or after a bad school result, and picks a calm Sunday afternoon, since timing changes how a request lands.

passage: I'm Suraj, and I learnt about timing by getting it wrong. The first time I asked Papa about the overnight trek with Sahil's family, it was a Thursday night. Papa had just come off a twelve-hour shift and was eating dinner standing up. He said no before I finished the sentence. The second time was worse: the day my Maths result came back with a 52. So I stopped and thought about it. The request was the same both times. Papa wasn't the problem; the moment was. He's always easiest on Sunday afternoons, after lunch, with the cricket on and nowhere to be. So I waited a whole week. That Sunday I sat next to him during a slow over and asked properly, with all the details. He listened to every word. He said he'd call Sahil's father.

qa.q: When did Suraj first ask Papa?
qa.a: On a Thursday night, after Papa's twelve-hour shift.

qa.q: Why did Suraj wait a whole week?
qa.a: Suraj felt it was worth being patient, seeing that Papa's tiredness, not the request, caused the quick no.

qa.q: What else could Suraj do to make the Sunday talk go well?
qa.a: Bring all the details, who is going, where they will stay and when they will be back, so Papa can say yes without worrying.

qa.q: What was the Thursday request like for Papa?
qa.a: Papa was exhausted after a twelve-hour shift and eating standing up, so a big request felt like one more burden, and he said no quickly.

grounding: A teen recalls avoiding asking when the father was tired or after a bad result and choosing a calm Sunday afternoon instead.

Counsellor's note, 10 October — Pranav, Class 11
Pranav came in frustrated last week: every time he asked his father about joining the weekend football league, the answer was no. We went through when he had asked. Monday, right after his father got home from the night shift. Then the evening the half-yearly Physics mark came in. Then during a family argument about bills. I asked what his father is like on a relaxed day. Pranav thought, then said, "Sunday morning, after his walk, when he reads the paper." He decided to try then, with the league timings written down. Today he told me it went differently. His father asked questions instead of saying no, and agreed to a trial month. Pranav said, "Same question. Different day."
— Uday

qa.q: When is Pranav's father most relaxed?
qa.a: Sunday morning, after his walk, when he reads the paper.

qa.q: How was Pranav feeling when he first came in?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and discouraged after repeated refusals.

qa.q: Why did choosing Sunday morning help?
qa.a: His father was calm and rested, so he could listen and ask questions instead of reacting from tiredness or stress.

qa.q: How might Pranav's father have experienced the earlier requests?
qa.a: He was tired from a night shift or upset about marks or bills, so the requests landed as extra pressure and got quick refusals.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teen moving his request away from tired or tense moments to a calm Sunday morning.
